text: Glasses and robots will watch for hours, and we'll ask them about what they saw.
But for a vision-language model, one hour of video is six and a half gigabytes of tokens.
Most memories cope by forgetting: they keep some frames in full and drop the rest.
Memryoshka stores each token as a nested code, a shorter code inside a longer one, just like Russian Matryoshka dolls.
As memory fills, one price per bit decides what to shorten and what to drop.
Here, forty-eight minutes of film stream into seven megabytes. Frames from start to finish stay in memory, at lower detail. At full precision, the same memory would hold three.
On six benchmarks it matches a memory that keeps everything, with about a thousand times less storage on hour-long videos, and beats existing memories by six to eight points.
It also works for robots, and for audio and video together.
No training needed. Memryoshka: fade, don't forget.
